adj:lose.tx: From Old High German lōs. Cognate with English loose.

adj:liberal.tx: From Latin līberālis (“befitting a freeman”), from līber (“free”).

adj:legal.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin lēgālis (“legal”), from lēx (“law”).

verb:landen.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German landen, derived from the cognate form of German Land (“land”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *land, from Proto-Germanic *landą, from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”). Replaced native länden.

adj:link.tx: From Middle High German linc, lënc, from Old High German *link, lënk (“left”); compare Old High German lënka (“the left hand”).

adj:langsam.tx: From Middle High German lancsam, from Old High German lancsam, from Proto-West Germanic *langasam (“lengthy, long-lasting”), equivalent to lang + -sam.

adv:langsam.tx: From Middle High German lancsam, from Old High German lancsam, from Proto-West Germanic *langasam (“lengthy, long-lasting”), equivalent to lang + -sam.

adj:ledig.tx: From Middle High German lëdic, lëdec, from Old High German *lidig, from Proto-Germanic *liþugaz.

adj:linear.tx: Borrowed from Latin līneāris. Doublet of lineal.

adv:links.tx: From Middle High German linkes, originally the genitive of linc, whence modern link; see there for more. Cognate with Dutch links. By surface analysis, link + -s.

noun:Lexikon.tx: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek λεξικόν (lexikón, “dictionary”), from λεξικός (lexikós)

verb:legen.tx: From Middle High German legen, from Old High German leggen, from Proto-West Germanic *laggjan, from Proto-Germanic *lagjaną. Compare English lay, Danish lægge.

adv:los.tx: Inherited from Middle High German and Old High German lōs. Compare English loose.

intj:los.tx: Inherited from Middle High German and Old High German lōs. Compare English loose.

noun:Leber.tx: From Middle High German lëbere, from Old High German lëbera, lëbara, from Proto-West Germanic *libru; akin to Dutch lever, English liver, Danish lever.

noun:Lyssa.tx: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek λύσσα (lússa).

adj:leer.tx: From Middle High German lēr, lēre, lǣre, from Old High German lāri, from Proto-West Germanic *lāʀi, from Proto-Germanic *lēziz. Cognate with Bavarian lar, Dutch laar, English leer.

noun:Licht.tx: From Middle High German lieht (Middle German also līcht), from Old High German lioht, from Proto-West Germanic *leuht, from Proto-Germanic *leuhtą, from Proto-Indo-European *lewktom. Compare Dutch licht, English light.

noun:Leiter.tx: From Middle High German leiter(e), from Old High German (h)leitara, from Proto-Germanic *hlaidrijō.

adj:lass.tx: From Middle High German laȥ, from Old High German laȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *lat, from Proto-Germanic *lataz. Cognate with English late.

noun:Liebe.tx: From Middle High German liebe (“joy, affection, kindliness”), from Old High German liob, lioba (“fortune, health, pleasantness, joy”), from Proto-West Germanic *leubu (“love”). Related with Old High German luba, English love (from Proto-Germanic *lubō).

verb:laden.tx: From Middle High German laden (strong verb), from Old High German hladan, from Proto-West Germanic *hlaþan. Compare English laden.

adj:loyal.tx: 18th century, from French loyal, from Latin legalis. Doublet of legal.

noun:Löwe.tx: From Middle High German lewe, löuwe, lauwe, from Old High German lewo, lēo, from Proto-West Germanic *lewo, *lēwo (“lion”). The spelling -ew- in Middle High German generally represents a diphthong [øy̯(w)], and accordingly the expected form in Modern German is Leu(e) (cf. freuen). The form Löwe with a monophthong and consonantal -w- is most readily explained from a long-vowel variant lēwe, which …

adj:lateral.tx: In the 20th century, from Latin laterālis.

verb:lieben.tx: Formally from Middle High German lieben, alteration (based on liep) of rarer liuben (“to make or be dear, to treat in a friendly way”), from Old High German liuben, equivalent to lieb + -en. The singularly attested Old High German liobōn (“to love”) probably remained without continuation; the modern sense was derived in late Middle High German from the noun liebe (“love”) on the model of minnen …

noun:Luke.tx: Borrowed from Low German, from Middle Low German lûke, from Old Saxon *lūka, from Proto-West Germanic *lūkā. Cognate with Dutch luik (“hatch”) and, more distantly, doublet of Loch (“hole”) and Lücke (“gap”); see the former for more.

verb:laufen.tx: From Middle High German loufen, from Old High German hloufan, loufan, from Proto-West Germanic *hlaupan. Cognate with Dutch lopen, English leap and lope, Danish løbe.

verb:lachen.tx: From Middle High German lachen, from Old High German hlahhen, from Proto-West Germanic *hlahhjan, from Proto-Germanic *hlahjaną.

adj:lang.tx: From Middle High German lanc, from Old High German lang, from Proto-West Germanic *lang, from Proto-Germanic *langaz.

adv:lang.tx: From Middle High German lanc, from Old High German lang, from Proto-West Germanic *lang, from Proto-Germanic *langaz.

prep:lang.tx: From Middle High German lanc, from Old High German lang, from Proto-West Germanic *lang, from Proto-Germanic *langaz.

noun:Lab.tx: From Middle High German lap, from Old High German lab, of uncertain origin. Possibly an alteration of Proto-Germanic *lubją (“sap, poison”).

noun:Labor.tx: Clipping of Laboratorium, from Latin labōrātōrium.

noun:Lack.tx: 16th century, from Italian lacca, from Arabic لَكّ (lakk), from Persian لاک (lâk), from Hindi लाख (lākh), from Sanskrit लाक्षा (lākṣā).

noun:Lade.tx: From Middle High German lade, Old High German *lada (“receptacle, chest”), ultimately from the root of laden (“to load”). Cognate with Middle English laþe, Old Norse hlaþa (“barn, storehouse”), English lathe.

noun:Laden.tx: From Middle High German laden, lade (“board; plank; shutter; shop”), from Old High German *lado, from Proto-West Germanic *laþō. Probably akin to German Latte, English lath. Unrelated to Lade.

noun:Lager.tx: From Middle High German lëger, from Old High German lëgar, from Proto-West Germanic *legr. Cognate with Dutch leger, Middle Low German lēger, English lair, Danish lejr, Norwegian Bokmål leir, Swedish läger (“place to sleep”) and lager (“storage, stock”), Gothic 𐌻𐌹𐌲𐍂𐍃 (ligrs). The modern form with -a- is of East Central German origin, apparently due to influence by the related word Lage. The …

noun:Lama.tx: From Spanish llama, from Quechua llama.

noun:Land.tx: From Middle High German lant, from Old High German lant, from Proto-West Germanic *land, from Proto-Germanic *landą, from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”). Compare Dutch, English, and Danish land, Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐌽𐌳 (land).

noun:Lasagne.tx: From Italian lasagne f pl (“lasagna”). The word is usually a plurale tantum in Italian, though a rarer singular lasagna exists. In German, the Italian plural form is used as a singular.

noun:Lasso.tx: Borrowed from English lasso, from Spanish lazo, from Vulgar Latin *laceum, from Latin laqueus. Doublet of Latz.

noun:Last.tx: From Middle High German last, from Old High German last, hlast, from Proto-West Germanic *hlasti, from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂- (“to put, lay out”), whence English laden. Compare English last and ballast.

noun:Laster.tx: From Middle High German laster, from Old High German lastar, from Proto-Germanic *lahstrą (with regular loss of h before st), a variant form of *lahtrą (whence Old English leahtor and Dutch lachter), from the root of *lahaną (“to blame, fault, reproach”) (whence also Old Norse lǫstr and its descendant Icelandic löstur), from Proto-Indo-European *lok-, whence also Old Irish locht.

noun:Latino.tx: Borrowed from English Latino, ultimately from Spanish latino. Doublet of Latein.

noun:Latrine.tx: Borrowed from French latrine (“latrine”), from Latin lātrīna.

noun:Latte.tx: From Middle High German latte, from Old High German latta, from Proto-West Germanic *lattu. Cognate with English lath, Dutch lat.

noun:Laudanum.tx: From New Latin, from Latin laudō (“to praise”), or ladanum (“a gum resin”), from Ancient Greek λάδανον (ládanon).

noun:Laus.tx: From Middle High German lūs, from Old High German lūs, from Proto-West Germanic *lūs, from Proto-Germanic *lūs.

noun:Lava.tx: 18th century, borrowed from Italian lava. See English lava for more.

noun:Lee.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German lē, from Old Saxon hlēo. Cognate with Dutch lij, English lee.

noun:Lehm.tx: From Middle High German leime, from Old High German leimo, from Proto-West Germanic *laimō, from Proto-Germanic *laimô, variant of *laimaz. The modern vocalism is Central and Low German; compare Middle Low German lêm, from Old Saxon lēmo. The regular form was replaced due to its becoming homophonous with the related Leim (“glue”).

noun:Lei.tx: From Middle High German leie, probably from Celtic and ultimately from a substrate language. Cognate with Luxembourgish Lee, Dutch lei.

noun:Lemming.tx: Ca. 1800, from Dano-Norwegian lemming, from Old Norse læmingi, læmingr, lómundr (“lemming”). Further origin unknown, perhaps from Sami luomek.

noun:Leo.tx: From Old High German lēo (“shelter”), from Proto-West Germanic *hlaiw.

noun:Leu.tx: From Middle High German lëwe, from Old High German leo, from Latin leo.

noun:Level.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English level. Doublet of Libelle and Niveau.

noun:Lid.tx: From Middle High German lit (“lid, cover”), from Old High German hlit, from Proto-West Germanic *hlid. In the modern sense a shortening of Augenlid. Cognate with Dutch lid (“lid”), English lid, Icelandic hlið.

noun:Lied.tx: From Middle High German liet, from Old High German liod (“song, lay, singing”), from Proto-West Germanic *leuþ (“song”), from Proto-Germanic *leuþą (“song”).

noun:Lift.tx: Late 19th century, unadapted borrowing from British English lift.

noun:Linguist.tx: Derived from Latin lingua (“language”) + -ist. Popularised in the 20th century under influence of English linguist, whence it may also have been borrowed in the 16th century.

noun:List.tx: From Middle High German list, from Old High German list, from Proto-West Germanic *listi, from Proto-Germanic *listiz. Cognate with English list (“craft, cunning”), which see for more.

noun:Liter.tx: Borrowed from French litre, from Ancient Greek λίτρα (lítra).

noun:Lithium.tx: Borrowed from New Latin lithium, from Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos, “stone”) as this element was the first alkali metal to be found in stones instead of plants.

noun:Lob.tx: From Middle High German lop, from Old High German lob, from Proto-West Germanic *lob, from Proto-Germanic *lubą. Cognate with Old English lof, Dutch lof, Swedish lov. More at lofe.

noun:Loch.tx: From Middle High German loch, from Old High German loh, from Proto-West Germanic *lok (“lock; hole”). Doublet of Lücke (“gap”) and Luke (“hatch”).

noun:Loge.tx: Borrowed from French loge. Doublet of Lobby and Loggia.

noun:Logik.tx: Borrowed from Latin logica, from Ancient Greek λογική (logikḗ, “logic”).

noun:Los.tx: From Middle High German lōȥ, from Old High German hlōȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *hlaut, from Proto-Germanic *hlaut-. This is an ablaut variant of *hlut-, whence Dutch lot, English lot, and extinct Middle High German luȥ, from Old High German hluȥ. The genders and stem forms of these variants vary greatly among the Germanic languages; in High German *hlaut- is an a-stem and predominantly neuter, …

noun:Lost.tx: From the surnames of the developers Lommel and Steinkopf.

noun:Lot.tx: Inherited from Middle High German lōt, from Old High German *lōt, from Proto-West Germanic *laud, possibly borrowed from Gaulish *loudon, from Proto-Celtic *ɸloudom (“lead”).

noun:Luft.tx: From Middle High German luft m or f, from Old High German luft, from Proto-West Germanic *luftu, from Proto-Germanic *luftuz. Compare Dutch lucht, Low German Lucht, Old English lyft, Danish luft, Swedish luft, Icelandic loft. The word was originally masculine in Upper German. The feminine is Central German, reinforced by Middle Low German luft, lucht f.

noun:Lulu.tx: From a diminutive of Luise and other female names beginning with Lu-.

noun:Lurch.tx: Borrowed from German Low German Lork (“toad”), of unknown origin, but possibly imitative. The form Lurch (also obsolete Lorch) is through secondary and inadequate adaptation to the phonetics of standard German.

noun:Lust.tx: From Middle High German lust, from Old High German lust, from Proto-West Germanic *lustu, from Proto-Germanic *lustuz. Cognate with English lust, West Frisian lust, Dutch lust.

noun:Lyra.tx: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek λύρα (lúra), whence also older Leier.

adj:locker.tx: From an adjectival form of Middle High German lücke / lugge, with further origin uncertain; perhaps related to Lücke (“gap”) and Loch (“hole”), via semantic development along the lines of "gap" > "loose opening" > "loose". Compare the semantics of English gap → gappy.

adv:locker.tx: From an adjectival form of Middle High German lücke / lugge, with further origin uncertain; perhaps related to Lücke (“gap”) and Loch (“hole”), via semantic development along the lines of "gap" > "loose opening" > "loose". Compare the semantics of English gap → gappy.

noun:Lichtjahr.tx: From Licht + Jahr, parallel to the formation of English light year.

adj:licht.tx: From Middle High German liecht, from Old High German lioht, from Proto-West Germanic *leuht, from Proto-Germanic *leuhtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-. Compare Dutch licht, English light.

verb:leiden.tx: From Middle High German līden, from Old High German līdan, from Proto-West Germanic *līþan, from Proto-Germanic *līþaną. Cognate with Dutch lijden, Low German lieden, English lithe. The sense developed from “go, travel” via “endure” to “suffer”. This happened under the influence of Middle High German leiden (“to be sorry, suffer, be hated”), from Old High German leidēn, from Proto-West Germanic …

noun:Lauch.tx: From Middle High German louch, from Old High German louh, from Proto-West Germanic *lauk, from Proto-Germanic *laukaz. Compare Low German Look, Dutch look, English leek, Danish løg, Swedish lök.

noun:Lerche.tx: From Middle High German lē̆rche, Old High German lērahha, from Proto-West Germanic *laiwaʀikā, from Proto-Germanic *laiwazikǭ (“lark”). Cognate with Old English lāwrice, Dutch leeuwerik, English lark.

noun:Lärche.tx: From Middle High German lerche, larche, from Old High German lerihha, from Proto-West Germanic *larikā (“larch”).

noun:Lauf.tx: From Middle High German louf, from Old High German hlouf; louf, from Proto-Germanic *hlaupą.

noun:Laufbahn.tx: Lauf + Bahn, semantic loan from French carrière, via Karriere.

noun:Lauffeuer.tx: From laufen + Feuer. Originally for the line of gunpowder used to explode something remotely, then figuratively used for any fire that propagates rapidly.

noun:Laib.tx: From Middle High German leip, from Old High German hleib, from Proto-West Germanic *hlaib. Cognate with English loaf, Polish chleb, Russian хлеб (xleb). The spelling with -ai- follows the old Upper German orthography; it was advocated by grammarians such as Johann Christoph Gottsched in order to distinguish from Leib (“body”).

noun:Lanthan.tx: From Ancient Greek λανθάνω (lanthánō, “to escape notice”) + -um (“a chemical element”), because it had gone long undetected in mineral ores.

verb:lassen.tx: From Middle High German lāȥen, lān, from Old High German lāȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *lātan (“to let, allow”), from Proto-Germanic *lētaną (“to leave behind, allow”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁d- (“to let, leave behind”). Cognates include Bavarian låssn, Dutch laten, English let.

adj:lässig.tx: Suffixed form in -ig of an older adjective lass (“languid, slothful, idle, weary”), from Old High German laȥ (“slow, sluggish”), from Proto-Germanic *lataz (“slow, weary”), from Proto-Indo-European *lad- (“slow, weary”). Akin to Old English læt (“slow, slack, lax, late”) (English late), Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐍄𐍃 (lats, “sluggish, weary”), Latin lassus (“tired”). More at late.

verb:lesen.tx: From Middle High German lësen, from Old High German lësan, from Proto-West Germanic *lesan, from Proto-Germanic *lesaną (“to gather”), from Proto-Indo-European *les- (“to gather”). Cognate with English lease (“to gather”) [with an obsolete meaning], cognate with Low German lesen (“to read”), Dutch lezen (“to read”), Afrikaans lees (“to read”).

verb:lächeln.tx: From Middle High German lecheln. By surface analysis, lachen + -eln.

verb:leben.tx: From Middle High German lëben and Old High German lëbēn, from Proto-West Germanic *libbjan, from Proto-Germanic *libjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“leave, cling, linger”). Cognate with Old Saxon libbian (Middle Low German leven, German Low German lęven, lewen (“to live”)), Dutch leven, English live, West Frisian libje, Old Norse lifa (Swedish leva), Gothic 𐌻𐌹𐌱𐌰𐌽 (liban).

verb:lenken.tx: From Middle High German lenken, from Old High German lanca, related to Gelenk. Compare English lank (related to link), Hunsrik lenke.

noun:Leberwurst.tx: From Middle High German *leberwurst, from Old High German lebarwurst (“liverwurst”), equivalent to Leber + Wurst.

noun:Lappen.tx: From Middle High German lappe, from Old High German lappo, from Proto-West Germanic *lappā (“cloth, rag, lobe”) of uncertain origin, possibly Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”). The form is remarkable because of the unshifted geminate -pp- (instead of expected Old High German *lapfo). Based on the supposedly invariable nature of the consonant shift, lappo would have to be an originally …

noun:Lappe.tx: From Swedish lapp. See also Lappland.

noun:Laube.tx: Middle High German loube, from Old High German louba, from Proto-West Germanic *laubijā.

noun:Laub.tx: From Old High German loup, from Proto-Germanic *laubą, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- (“peel, break off”). Compare Low German Loov, Dutch loof, English leaf, Danish løv.

noun:Laubfrosch.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German [Term?]; Laub + Frosch.

verb:lutschen.tx: Ostensibly of onomatopoeic origin. Compare Dutch lutten (“to suck, to drink”).

noun:Leier.tx: From Middle High German līre, from Old High German līra, from Latin lyra, from Ancient Greek λύρα (lúra).

noun:Libelle.tx: From New Latin lībellula, coined by Carl von Linné after lībella (“carpenter's level”), because of the insect's ability to stay level when hovering. German Libelle is a shortened form, in part after the underlying Latin noun. Doublet of Niveau and Level.

noun:Luchs.tx: From Middle High German luhs, from Old High German luhs, from Proto-West Germanic *luhs.

noun:Leim.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German līm, from Proto-West Germanic *līm, from Proto-Germanic *līmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *sley- (“smooth; slick; sticky; slimy”) (modern English slime). Cognate with English lime.

noun:Lampe.tx: From Middle High German lampe, from Latin lampada, from Latin lampas. Cognate with English lamp.

noun:Lachs.tx: From Middle High German lahs, from Old High German lahs, from Proto-West Germanic *lahs, from Proto-Germanic *lahsaz.

noun:Laterne.tx: From Middle High German laterne, lanterne, from Latin lanterna with possible influence from French lanterne, from Ancient Greek λαμπτήρ (lamptḗr).

verb:liken.tx: Borrowed from English like + -en, equivalent to Like + -en.

adj:lind.tx: From Middle High German lint, linde, from Old High German lind, lindi, from Proto-West Germanic *linþ(ī), from Proto-Germanic *linþaz. Cognate with English lithe.

verb:liegen.tx: From Middle High German ligen, from Old High German ligen, from older liggen by generalisation of the stem of the 2nd and 3rd persons singular, from Proto-West Germanic *liggjan, from Proto-Germanic *ligjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ-. Compare Low German liggen, Dutch liggen, English lie, Danish ligge, Gothic 𐌻𐌹𐌲𐌰𐌽 (ligan).

adv:lange.tx: Inherited from Middle High German lange and Old High German lango, an adverb to Middle High German lanc, Old High German lang.

noun:Leiche.tx: Inherited from Middle High German līche, from Old High German līh, from Proto-West Germanic *līk, from Proto-Germanic *līką, from Proto-Indo-European *leyg-. Cognate with Luxembourgish Läich, English lich, Dutch lijk, Old Norse lík, Gothic 𐌻𐌴𐌹𐌺 (leik). Related to German gleich, English like and German -lich, English -ly.

noun:Laut.tx: From Middle High German lūt, from Old High German lūt, hlūt m, from Proto-West Germanic *hlūd m or n (“sound”), derived from the adjective Proto-Germanic *hlūdaz (“loud”). Cognate with Dutch luid, geluid, Middle Low German lût, Old Frisian hlūd. Different formations from the same root are Old English hlȳd and Old Norse hljóð (whence Danish lyd etc.).

adj:laut.tx: From Middle High German lūt, from Old High German lūt, akin to Old Saxon hlūd, from Proto-West Germanic *hlūd.

prep:laut.tx: Ellipsis of Middle High German nāh lūt, alternatively nach lūte, with the modern German meaning of nach dem Wortlaut (“according to the wording”).

noun:Lunge.tx: From Middle High German lunge, from Old High German lunga, from Proto-Germanic *lungô (literally “the light organ”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ- (“light, agile, nimble”). Compare Dutch long, English lung, Danish lunge, Swedish lunga, Icelandic lunga.

adj:leicht.tx: From Middle High German līht, from Old High German līht, from Proto-West Germanic *lį̄ht, from Proto-Germanic *linhtaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ-. Compare English light, Dutch licht, Danish let.

adv:leicht.tx: From Middle High German līht, from Old High German līht, from Proto-West Germanic *lį̄ht, from Proto-Germanic *linhtaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ-. Compare English light, Dutch licht, Danish let.

verb:labern.tx: An originally Central and Low German verb, from Middle Low German labbern (“to drink like a dog; to slurp”). Related to laff (“slack”, here of the tongue).

adj:lineal.tx: From Latin līneālis. Doublet of linear.

noun:Locke.tx: From the plural of earlier Lock m, from Middle High German loc, from Old High German loc, from Proto-West Germanic *lukk, from Proto-Germanic *lukkaz. Cognate with Dutch lok, English lock, Danish lok.

verb:leiten.tx: From Middle High German leiten, from Old High German leiten, from Proto-West Germanic *laidijan, akin to Old English lǣdan (English lead), Old Saxon lēdian, Old Norse leiða. Cognate with English lead.

noun:Leute.tx: From Middle High German liute, from Old High German liuti, also liudi, from Proto-West Germanic *liud(i), from Proto-Germanic *liudīz (“people”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ- (“man, people”). Compare Dutch lieden, luden, luiden, Old Norse lýðir (“people”) (whence Icelandic lýður), Old Saxon liudi, Old English lēode (“people”), English lede (“people”), Gothic *𐌻𐌹𐌿𐌸𐍃 (*liuþs), Polish ludzie, …

noun:Löffel.tx: From Middle High German leffel, from Old High German leffil, attested as earlier ᛚᚨᛈᛖᛚᚨ (lapela), from Proto-West Germanic *lapil, from Proto-Germanic *lapilaz (“spoon”), ultimately derived from *lap- (“to lick; to lap”). See English lap. Cognates include Dutch lepel, Yiddish לעפֿל (lefl).

noun:Leder.tx: From Middle High German lëder, from Old High German lëdar, from Proto-West Germanic *leþr, from Proto-Germanic *leþrą (“leather”). Akin to Old Saxon lethar.

noun:Lamm.tx: Inherited from Middle High German lamp, in the 14th century also lam, from Old High German lamb, from Proto-West Germanic *lamb, from Proto-Germanic *lambaz. The loss of the b is reflective of a common trend in West Germanic languages; cognate with Dutch lam, Yiddish לאַם (lam), and the pronunciation of English lamb.

adv:leider.tx: From Middle High German leider, from Old High German leidir, equivalent to the comparative form of leid.

noun:Liedermacher.tx: From Lied (“song”) + -er- + Macher (“maker”). In the current sense popularized in the 1960s by Wolf Biermann.

adj:legitim.tx: 18th century, from Latin lēgitimus in legal parlance. The form (especially the final stress) is probably influenced by French légitime.

adj:lahm.tx: From Middle High German lam, from Old High German lam, from Proto-West Germanic *lam, from Proto-Germanic *lamaz.

noun:Lauge.tx: From Middle High German louge, from Old High German louga, from Proto-West Germanic *laugu, from Proto-Germanic *laugō.

noun:Lektion.tx: From Middle High German lectiōn (13th c.), relatinized form of older lecze, letze, from Old High German lekza (9th c.), a borrowing from Latin lēctiō. Compare Dutch les, Swedish läxa.

noun:Lebenslauf.tx: From Leben + -s- + Lauf, a calque of Latin curriculum vītae. Similar to Dutch levensloop.

noun:Leitung.tx: From leiten + -ung. Cognate with English leading.

verb:leihen.tx: From Middle High German līhen, from Old High German līhan, from Proto-West Germanic *līhwan, from Proto-Germanic *līhwaną.

noun:Leben.tx: From Middle High German lëben, from Old High German lëbēn. Equivalent to a gerund of leben.

noun:Lache.tx: From Middle High German lache, from Old High German lacha, lahha (“swamp, marsh”), from Proto-West Germanic *laku. The same word in a Low German form is Lake (“brine”), from Middle Low German lāke (“standing water; brine”), the latter of which seems also to have triggered the lengthened pronunciation of the -a- in Lache. Further cognates include Dutch laak (“lake, pond, stream”), Old English lacu …

noun:Lage.tx: From Middle High German lāge (“state of lying, reclining; esp. in ambush; situation; storehouse”), from Old High German lāga (“state of lying; ambush”). By surface analysis, deverbal from liegen. Related to Lager (“storeroom; camp”), Liege f (“daybed”). Compare English lie as in the lie of the land. Compare analog Nordic lægi (“location, position; situation, opportunity”), nominalization of the …

noun:Laken.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German lāken, from Old Saxon lakan, from Proto-Germanic *lakaną (“sheet, cloth”). The High German cognate Middle High German lachen, from Old High German lahhan, had already been declining in use when the form Laken was introduced during the pre-eminence of the Dutch and Northern German cloth industry (14th/15th centuries). Cognate with Dutch laken.

noun:Länge.tx: From Middle High German lenge, from Old High German lengī, from Proto-West Germanic *langī, from Proto-Germanic *langį̄ = *langaz + *-į̄; equivalent to lang + -e.

noun:Lärm.tx: From older Lärmen, from early modern lerma, lerman, larman, shortened from Alarm, ultimately from Italian allarme. Doublet of Alarm.

noun:Laune.tx: Via Middle High German lūne (“moon, changing mood, disposition”), borrowed from Latin lūna (“moon”). The semantic association of "moon" to "mood" is based on the similarity of the changing phases of the moon to the changing moods of a person (DWDS).

noun:Lawine.tx: From Alemannic German Lauwin, from Middle High German lowin, *lawene (compare Bavarian Laun, Lan), from Old High German lowin, lewina, from Late Latin labina, from Latin lābī (“to glide”).

verb:lecken.tx: From Middle High German lëcken, from Old High German lecchōn, from Proto-West Germanic *likkōn, from Proto-Germanic *likkōną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵʰ-. Cognate with Dutch likken, English lick, Latin lingō, Ancient Greek λείχω (leíkhō).

verb:lehnen.tx: From a merger of two interrelated verbs: # Middle High German linen, lenen, from Old High German hlinēn, from Proto-West Germanic *hlinēn, from Proto-Germanic *hlināną # Middle High German leinen, from Old High German hleinen, from Proto-West Germanic *hlainijan, from Proto-Germanic *hlainijaną, a causative of the former. This merger began in certain Central and Low German dialects in which -ei- …

noun:Lehre.tx: From Middle High German lēre, from Old High German lēra, from Proto-West Germanic *laiʀu, from Proto-Germanic *laizō, from *laizijaną. Akin to Dutch leer, English lore, Swedish lära. Related to German lehren and lernen.

verb:lehren.tx: From Middle High German lēren, from Old High German lēren, from Proto-West Germanic *laiʀijan, from *laizō (“lore”), from Proto-Germanic *laizijaną, from *lizaną + *-janą, stative from the root *leys- (“track, furrow, trace, trail”). Cognate with Alemannic German lehre, Low German lehren, Dutch leren, Afrikaans leer, Danish lære, Norwegian lære, Swedish lära, English lear. Related to lernen.

noun:Leib.tx: From Middle High German līp, from Old High German līb, from Proto-West Germanic *līb, from Proto-Germanic *lībą (“life, body”), from *lībaną (“to remain, stay, be left”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick, glue”). Cognate with Dutch lijf (“body”), Low German Lief (“body”), English life, Swedish liv (“life, waist”).

noun:Leine.tx: From Middle High German līne, from Old High German līna, from Proto-Germanic *līnǭ (“rope, string”).

noun:Lein.tx: From Middle High German līn, from Old High German līn, from Proto-West Germanic *līn.

noun:Leiste.tx: From Middle High German līste, from Old High German līsta, from Proto-West Germanic *līstā. Doublet of Liste.

verb:leisten.tx: From Middle High German leisten, from Old High German leisten, from Proto-West Germanic *laistijan. Cognate with English last.

noun:Lende.tx: From Middle High German lende, lente, from Old High German lentī, from Proto-Germanic *landį̄.

verb:lernen.tx: From Middle High German lernen, from Old High German lernēn, lirnēn, from Proto-West Germanic *liʀnēn. Cognate with Old English leornian (Modern English learn). Related to lehren.

verb:leuchten.tx: From Old High German liuhten, from Proto-West Germanic *liuhtijan, from Proto-Germanic *liuhtijaną.

verb:leugnen.tx: From Middle High German lougenen, lougen, from Old High German lougnen, louganen, from Proto-West Germanic *laugnijan, from Proto-Germanic *laugnijaną. Factitive of lügen (“to lie”).

noun:Linde.tx: From Middle High German linde, linte, from Old High German linta, from Proto-West Germanic *lindu.

noun:Lippe.tx: An originally Low and Central German form (though not in all dialects of the latter). From Middle Low German lippe and northern Middle High German lippe, from Old High German *lippa, from Proto-West Germanic *lippjō. One reason for the form’s prevailing in modern standard German was its use in Luther’s Bible translation. It gradually reduced Upper German Lefze to a marginal role (now chiefly “lip …

noun:Liste.tx: 16th century, from Italian lista, itself of Germanic origin, whence also the inherited doublet Leiste (“skirting board”). Cognate with Dutch lijst and English list.

noun:Lohn.tx: From Middle High German lôn, from Old High German lōn, from Proto-West Germanic *laun, from Proto-Germanic *launą, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂w-. Cognate with Old English lēan.

noun:Lorbeer.tx: From Middle High German lōrber, from Old High German lōrberi, from lōr (“laurel”) + beri (“berry”), the former from Latin laurus. The compound originally referred to the laurel's fruit or berry, which is now distinguished as Lorbeere (but fairly rare).

noun:Lücke.tx: From Middle High German lücke, lucke, from Old High German luccha (“gap, space, opening, slit, crack, hatch”), from Proto-West Germanic *lukkjā (“hatch, trap door”), from Proto-Germanic *lukjǭ (“hole, opening, gap”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewg- (“to bend”). Doublet of Loch (“hole”) and Luke (“hatch”), and see the former for more.

noun:Lüge.tx: From Middle High German lüge, from Old High German lugī, from the root of lügen (“to lie”). Merged with related Middle High German lügen(e), from Old High German lugina, from Proto-West Germanic *luginu. With the latter are cognate Yiddish ליגן (lign), Luxembourgish Ligen, Dutch leugen, Low German Lögen. The two forms were bound to merge as all Middle High German feminines in -en(e) end in -e in modern German.

noun:Lump.tx: Originally the same as Lumpen (“rag, tatter”), later distinguished in form.

noun:Lumpen.tx: From Middle High German lumpe. Lump (“cad”) is originally the same word. Compare German Lappen (“cloth, rag”) as well as the now obsolete verbs lampen (“to hang limply”), lumpen (“to hang limply, to limp”) and English limp, all probably from Proto-Germanic *limpaną (“to glide, go, suit”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)lemb-, *(s)lembʰ- (“to hang loosely, hang limply”). Compare Sanskrit …

noun:Lenz.tx: From Middle High German lenze, from Old High German lenzo, from Proto-West Germanic *langatīn. Related to English Lent and Dutch lente.

noun:Leichnam.tx: From Middle High German līchname, from Old High German līhhinhamo, a chiefly Bavarian byform of līhhamo, from Proto-West Germanic *līkahamō. Cognate with Dutch lichaam, Old English līchama, whence English likam (“corpse”).

verb:löschen.tx: From Middle High German leschen, from Old High German lescan, from Proto-West Germanic *leskan, from Proto-Germanic *leskaną. Cognate with Dutch lessen.

adj:lau.tx: From Middle High German lā (inflected lāwe), from Old High German lāo, from Proto-West Germanic *hlāu, from Proto-Germanic *hlēwaz. Cognate with Dutch lauw. Also related to English lukewarm.

adj:leck.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German leck, derived from the verb lecken (“to leak”). Compare Dutch lek.

adj:leid.tx: From Middle High German leit from Old High German leid, from Proto-West Germanic *laiþ, whence also English loath and Old Norse leiðr; also Latin laedō (“strike, betray”).

adj:leise.tx: From Middle High German līse (also linse), from Old High German *līsi, from Proto-West Germanic *līs(ī) (“low, soft, gentle”).

adv:leise.tx: From Middle High German līse (also līs, līnse), from Old High German līso, from Proto-West Germanic *līsō, *līsijō, from the adjective (see above).

adj:lieb.tx: From Middle High German liep, from Old High German liob, from Proto-West Germanic *leub. Compare Dutch lief, archaic English lief.

verb:lügen.tx: From Middle High German liegen, from Old High German liogan, from Proto-West Germanic *leugan, from Proto-Germanic *leuganą, from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ-. Cognate with Bavarian liagn, Dutch liegen, Low German liegen, legen, lögen, English lie, Danish lyve, Swedish ljuga. The expected form is Early Modern German liegen; that with -ü- has been standardized to avoid homophony with unrelated …

verb:locken.tx: From Middle High German locken, from Old High German lockōn, from Proto-West Germanic *lokkōn, from Proto-Germanic *lukkōną. Cognate with lügen (“to lie”), Latin laciō and Slovak lákať (“to allure”).

adj:lustig.tx: From Middle High German lustec, from Old High German lustīg. By surface analysis, Lust (“pleasure, joy; wish”) + -ig (“-y”).

noun:Läufer.tx: From Middle High German löufer, löufære, from Old High German loufāri, loupfāri, equivalent to laufen + -er. Compare Dutch loper, English leaper.

adj:lapidar.tx: 18th century, from Latin lapidarius, after French lapidaire.

noun:Limoncello.tx: Borrowed from Italian limoncello, from limone (“lemon”).

noun:Lacrosse.tx: Borrowed from English lacrosse; from French lacrosse; from la + crosse.

noun:Lobby.tx: Borrowed from English lobby. Doublet of Loggia.

noun:Linie.tx: From Middle High German linie, from Medieval Latin linea, alternative form of older Latin līnea. Earlier borrowings from the same source, such as Old High German linna, were not continued.

noun:Lanze.tx: From Middle High German lanze, borrowed from Old French lance.

noun:Löwenzahn.tx: In the literal sense inherited from Middle High German lewenzan, equivalent to Löwe (“lion”) + -n- + Zahn (“tooth”). The botanic sense is a 16th-century calque of Latin dēns leōnis, whence also English dandelion.

noun:Lautsprecher.tx: From laut (“loud”) + Sprecher (“speaker”), a calque of English loudspeaker.

adj:lecker.tx: From Middle High German lecker, from Old High German *lekkar, from Proto-West Germanic *likkr, derived from the verb Proto-West Germanic *likkōn (“to lick”). Cognate to Dutch lekker, Afrikaans lekker, Middle Low German lecker, Norwegian lekker, Swedish läcker and Danish lækker. More at lick.

adv:lecker.tx: From Middle High German lecker, from Old High German *lekkar, from Proto-West Germanic *likkr, derived from the verb Proto-West Germanic *likkōn (“to lick”). Cognate to Dutch lekker, Afrikaans lekker, Middle Low German lecker, Norwegian lekker, Swedish läcker and Danish lækker. More at lick.

noun:Lilie.tx: From Middle High German lilje, from Old High German lilia, from Latin lilia.

adj:langweilig.tx: From Langeweile + -ig, from lang (“long”, adjective) + Weile (“while”, noun) + -ig. Cognate with Hunsrik langweilich.

noun:Lotterie.tx: 16th century, borrowed along the Lower Rhine from Dutch loterye, lottrie (modern loterij), from Middle Dutch loterye (mid-15th c.), derived from lot, which is related with German Los. The Dutch word originated from the bilingual contact zones of Flanders and may be a Frenchified form of earlier Middle Dutch lotinghe (German Losung). Compare French loterie (16th c.).

verb:leeren.tx: From Middle High German læren, from Old High German *lāren (attested as irlāren). By surface analysis, leer + -en.

noun:Liebstöckel.tx: From Middle High German liebstockel, liebstuckel, lubestuckel, from Old High German lubistuckil, lubistehhal, from Proto-West Germanic *lubistukil, *lubistikil (“lovage”).

adj:lieblich.tx: By surface analysis, lieb + -lich. Diachronically, Middle High German lieplich, from Old High German liublīh, lioblīh, from Proto-West Germanic *leubalīk, from Proto-Germanic *leubalīkaz. Cognate with Dutch lieflijk, Gothic 𐌻𐌹𐌿𐌱𐌰𐌻𐌴𐌹𐌺𐍃 (liubaleiks).

noun:Losung.tx: From Middle High German losunge equivalent to Los (“lot”) + -ung.

verb:lochen.tx: From Middle High German lochen (“to punch”), equivalent to Loch + -en.

noun:Lippenstift.tx: From Lippe (“lip”) + -n- + Stift (“stick”), a calque of English lipstick. Compare Dutch lippenstift (alongside lipstick).

noun:Leidenschaft.tx: 17th century, from Leiden (“suffering”) + -schaft, a calque of Latin passio. Compare Dutch lijdenschap.

noun:Leitungswasser.tx: From Leitung (“water conduit, water pipe”) + -s- + Wasser (“water”).

adj:luxuriös.tx: Borrowed from French luxurieux, from Latin lūxuriōsus.

adj:lausig.tx: Laus (“louse”) + -ig (“-y”), thus "evocative of lice" > "very bad". Cognate with English lousy.

adj:lokal.tx: From Latin locālis (“local”), from locus (“place, spot, location”).

noun:Lokal.tx: Borrowed from French local, from Latin localis.

verb:lüften.tx: From Middle High German lüften (“to lift into the air”), from Old High German luftēn, from Proto-Germanic *luftijaną. More at lift.

noun:Linse.tx: From Middle High German linse, from Old High German linsa, likely a borrowing from an unidentified source. Compare Latin lēns, Lithuanian lęšis, and Old Church Slavonic лѧща (lęšta) sounding too similar for a coincidence, however different enough to prohibit reconstruction of a common PIE protoform. If ultimately a non-IE loanword, locating the source is virtually impossible because cultivation …

adj:lächerlich.tx: From Middle High German lecherlich. Equivalent to lachen + -er- + -lich.

noun:Lösung.tx: From Middle High German lœsunge, lōsunge, from Old High German lōsunga (“redemption, payment, ransom, fraud, deception”), from Proto-West Germanic *lausungu, from Proto-Germanic *lausungō, equivalent to lösen + -ung. Cognate with English leasing, Alemannic German Lösig, Icelandic lausung. Compare also Dutch oplossing.

verb:lösen.tx: From Middle High German lœsen, lōsen, from Old High German lōsen, from Proto-West Germanic *lausijan. Cognate with Dutch lozen, English loose (from Old Norse lauss), obsolete English leese (from Old English līesan); also Danish løse, Faroese loysa, Icelandic leysa (“to loosen, to resolve, to untie”), Norwegian løse and Swedish lösa (all from the Old Norse leysa).

verb:lasten.tx: From Middle High German lesten, ultimately from the root of Last (“burden, load”).

noun:Legende.tx: From Middle High German legende (“story of a saint”), from Late Latin legenda.

noun:Leinwand.tx: From Middle High German līnwāt (“linen”), reshaped under influence of Gewand (“garment”); compare Middle High German līngewant.

noun:Leuchtturm.tx: 17th century, from leuchten (“to shine, light up”) + Turm (“tower”)

noun:Linguistik.tx: From Linguist + -ik, akin to earlier Latin linguisticus (“linguistic”), likely coined by Austrian bibliographer Michael Denis in 1770s.

adv:längs.tx: From Middle High German langes, lenges. Equivalent to lang + -s.

prep:längs.tx: From Middle High German langes, lenges. Equivalent to lang + -s.

noun:Laute.tx: From Middle High German lūte (14th c.), from Old French leüt, from Old Spanish laúd, alod, from Arabic اَلْعُود (al-ʕūd).

noun:Liebhaber.tx: Derived from liebhaben (“to love”) + -er. Compare Dutch liefhebber.

noun:Logbuch.tx: Since 1757. Partial calque of English logbook, synchronically compound of Log (“log, instrument for measuring speed at sea”) + Buch (“book”).

noun:Labe.tx: From Middle High German labe, from Old High German laba (“refreshment, relief, rescue”), from Proto-West Germanic *labu, from Proto-West Germanic *labōn (“to refresh”). Cognate with Middle Low German lāve (“refreshment, restoration, joy”).

noun:Laktose.tx: Borrowed from French lactose, formed from Latin lac (“milk”) + -ose (“sugar”) (derivation of sucrose).

noun:Lepra.tx: Borrowed from Latin lepra or Koine Greek λέπρα (lépra).

verb:lauschen.tx: From Middle High German lūschen, akin to Middle Low German lûschen, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *hlūd (“loud”), compare English listen.

noun:Lebkuchen.tx: From 13th-century Middle High German lebekuoche. The second element is clearly Kuchen; the origin of the first element is uncertain: it might come from the same root as Laib (“loaf”), or from Latin libum (“flat bread”) (for the unexpected vowel, compare Middle High German lebezelte, which existed alongside the form with the expected vowel, libenzelte), though both theories present difficulties.

noun:Leberkäse.tx: The first part is probably either from Middle High German leiba (“remainder”), lab (“to clot”) or German Laib (“loaf”); the second part is Käse (“cheese”), although it seems to come originally from Kasten (“box”). By folk etymology it was interpreted as Leber (“liver”) + Käse (“cheese”), for which reason liver (and even cheese) are sometimes added to the dish.

adj:laff.tx: Borrowed from Low German laff, which is either inherited from Middle Low German *laf (seemingly not attested) or borrowed from Middle Dutch laf (early 15th century), all probably from Proto-Germanic *laba-, from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”). Compare modern Dutch laf (“cowardly”).

noun:Lineal.tx: 15th century, learned borrowing from Latin līneāle.

noun:Leck.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German lek, a nominalization of the adjective leck (“leaky”).

noun:Larve.tx: From Middle High German larve, from Latin lārva (“ghost; mask”).

adj:lateinisch.tx: From Latein + -isch or from Middle High German latīnisch.

noun:Lektüre.tx: Borrowed from French lecture, from Latin lēctūra.

verb:lancieren.tx: From French lancer + -ieren. Doublet of launchen.

noun:Leiden.tx: Gerund of leiden (“to bear, to endure, to suffer”), a cognate of English lithe.

adj:lebendig.tx: From Middle High German lëbendic, from Old High German lëbēntīg. Equivalent to lebend + -ig. The word originally had normal stress on the initial syllable, as is still the case in Dutch levendig, Yiddish לעבעדיק (lebedik), and in some dialectal German forms such as Hunsrik levendich. The shift to the second syllable is first attested in the 16th century; it had established itself as the sole …

noun:Lindwurm.tx: From Middle High German lintwurm, from Old High German lindwurm, lintwurm, from Proto-West Germanic *linþawurmi, from Proto-Germanic *linþawurmiz. By surface analysis, lind + Wurm.

adj:liebenswert.tx: From lieben (“to love”) + -s- + -wert (“-worthy”), literally “love-worthy, worthy to be loved”.

verb:liieren.tx: Borrowed from French lier, late 18th c.

noun:Leitfaden.tx: leiten + Faden, in reference to Ariadnefaden (“Ariadne's thread”).

noun:Liga.tx: Borrowed from Italian lega and Spanish liga, both derived from Latin ligō (“to tie”).

adj:leidig.tx: Inherited from Middle High German leidic, leidec, from Old High German leidīg. Equivalent to Leid + -ig. Cognate with archaic English loathy.

noun:Leid.tx: From Middle High German leit, from Old High German leid, from Proto-Germanic *laiþą, related to *laiþaz (“loath”). Cognate with Dutch leed, English loath. Originally unrelated with the verb leiden (“to suffer”), though the two stems early on began to influence each other. See leid for more.

noun:Lette.tx: Ultimately from Latvian latvis. The e-vocalism might be generalized from the adjective lettisch (lättisch).

verb:liefern.tx: From Middle High German lieveren (before 1350), which may be borrowed directly from Old French livrer, from Latin līberō, but was probably introduced via Middle Dutch and Middle Low German lēveren (the vocalism -ie- then being due to hypercorrection; compare also attested liebern). Low German definitely contributed to the spread of the word, which was part of the technical vocabulary of the …

verb:löten.tx: From Middle High German lœten, ultimately from the root of Lot (“lead, solder, unit of weight”).

noun:Lotse.tx: Shortened from earlier Lootsmann, which is borrowed via Middle Low German lōtsman from Middle English lodesman (“pilot”), cognate with English lode (“waterway”). Compare Dutch loods from the same source.

noun:Lösegeld.tx: From lösen (“to loosen, let go of”) + Geld (“money”).

noun:Loyalität.tx: From French loyauté, ultimately from Latin lēgālis (“legal”).

noun:Liebestod.tx: Liebe + -s- + Tod, from Richard Wagner's opera Tristan und Isolde (1865).

verb:loben.tx: From Middle High German loben, from Old High German lobēn or lobōn. Cognate with Old English lofian, Old Norse lofa, Low German löven, Dutch loven, Swedish lova. More at lofe. The verb loben is related to the noun Lob. It is not clear if the verb is derived from the noun or vice versa.

verb:lampen.tx: Nasal variant of laff, Lappen, labberig etc.

noun:Logis.tx: Borrowed from French logis m (“lodge”) in the 17th century.

noun:Lügner.tx: From Old High German lugināri, derived from the noun lugina (“lie”), from Proto-Germanic *luginō, cognate with Old Saxon lugina, Old English lyġen, derived from the verb *leuganą (“to lie”). lügen + -er

noun:Landwirt.tx: Land (“land”) + Wirt (“host; caretaker”). Chiefly a backformation from Landwirtschaft (“agriculture”).

adj:lüstern.tx: From lüsternd, ultimately from Old High German lusten.

adj:lupenrein.tx: From Lupe (“magnifying glass”) + rein (“clean, pure”), 1890s, univerbation of the phrase unter der Lupe rein (“pure under the magnifying glass”), 1850s; figurative use in the 20th century.

noun:Laie.tx: From Middle High German leie, leige, from Old High German leigo, a borrowing of Latin lāicus.

noun:Lappalie.tx: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from Lappen (“cloth, rag”) + Latin -ālia (neuter plural of relational adjective suffix), 17th c.. Initially as the plural Lappalia, then showing the Germanized plural Lappalien, then back-forming a feminine singular.

adj:lauter.tx: From Middle High German lūter (“clean, clear, pure”), from Old High German hlūtar, from Proto-West Germanic *hlūtr.

adv:lauter.tx: From Middle High German lūter (“clean, clear, pure”), from Old High German hlūtar, from Proto-West Germanic *hlūtr.

noun:Leguan.tx: Borrowed from Dutch leguaan. Ultimately from Taíno *iwana.

noun:Lavendel.tx: From Middle High German lavendel(e), from Old High German lavendula (10th c.), from Medieval Latin lavendula.

noun:Lecker.tx: From Middle High German lecker, leckære, from Old High German leckāri, lekkāri, lecchāri, equivalent to lecken + -er. Cognate with English licker.

verb:lullen.tx: Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂- (expressive root). Cognate with Latin lāmentum, Ancient Greek λῆρος (lêros), λάλος (lálos), λάσκω (láskō).

noun:Liebling.tx: From Liebe + -ling or lieb + -ling or lieben + -ling. Compare Middle High German liebelīn (“darling”), whence German Liebelein.

noun:Landratte.tx: From Land (“land”) + Ratte (“rat”), probably formed as an antonym to Wasserratte. According to Duden, a 19th century calque of English landrat, though the earliest attestation seems to be slightly earlier, in a 1789 play by Kotzebue.

noun:Lebensraum.tx: Leben (“life”) + -s- + Raum (“space”). The historical sense is attributed to Friedrich Ratzel.

noun:Landschaft.tx: From Middle High German lantschaft, from Old High German lantskaf. By surface analysis, Land + -schaft.

noun:Landwirtschaft.tx: From Land (“land”) + Wirtschaft (“householding, economy”). Also analysable as Landwirt (“farmer”) + -schaft (“-ship”).

verb:lichten.tx: Derived from the adjective licht (“light; bright”) and/or the noun Licht (“light”). Compare Hunsrik leichte.

noun:Ladung.tx: From Middle High German ladunge, from Old High German ladunga. By surface analysis, laden + -ung; cognate with Hunsrik Laadung

noun:Lila.tx: From older Lilas, from French lilas.

noun:Leisten.tx: From Middle High German leist (“foot trace, last”), from Old High German leist (“foot trace, last”), from Proto-Germanic *laistaz. Cognate with Dutch leest, English last, Swedish läst. The originally strong noun became weak in Early Modern German (der Leiste) and then strong again through generalisation of oblique -en (as usual in inanimate nouns).

noun:Lachgas.tx: From lachen (“to laugh”) + Gas (“gas”), calque of English laughing gas.

noun:Letten.tx: From Middle High German lette, from Old High German letto, from Proto-Germanic *ladjō-, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂t- (“moist, wet”). Cognate with Icelandic leðja (“mud, muck”), Welsh llaid (“mire”), Lithuanian latakas (“gutter”), and possibly Latin latex.

noun:Latz.tx: Ultimately from Latin laqueus. Doublet of Lasso.

noun:Laserdrucker.tx: Laser + Drucker, a calque of English laser printer.

adj:logisch.tx: From Latin logicus, with assimilation to native suffix -isch.

adv:logisch.tx: From Latin logicus, with assimilation to native suffix -isch.

verb:lauern.tx: From Middle High German lūren; related to English lour, Dutch loeren, Swedish lura, Danish lure.

verb:lähmen.tx: From Middle High German lemen, lemmen, from Old High German lemmen, from Proto-Germanic *lamjaną, derived from *lamaz (“lame”), whence German lahm (“lame”). The simplification of the geminate and subsequent lengthening of the vowel by analogy with this underlying adjective.

verb:lohnen.tx: From Middle High German lōnen, from Old High German lōnōn, from Proto-West Germanic *launōn. By surface analysis, Lohn + -en.

noun:Langschwert.tx: From lang (“long”) + Schwert (“sword”); univerbation of indefinite ein lang Schwert (17th century) to definite das Langschwert by the 1830s. In recent usage (2000s) also of the Renaissance-era two-handed bastard-sword or "longsword".

noun:Luv.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German lōf. The contemporary vocalism may be due to the influence of the cognate Dutch loef. See English luff for more.

adj:labil.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin lābilis (“slippery”), from lābor, lābī (“slip; glide, flow”).

verb:lenzen.tx: From Middle High German lenzen, from lenze (“spring”).

noun:Lügendetektor.tx: From Lüge + -n- + Detektor, after English lie detector.

adj:lyrisch.tx: From French lyrique, from Ancient Greek λυρικός (lurikós), with -isch instead of -ique / -ικός (-ikós). Morphologically analyzable as Lyrik + -isch.

noun:Lazarett.tx: 16th century, from Italian lazzaretto, in part through French lazaret.

adj:lieferbar.tx: Derived from the verb liefern: liefer- (“deliver”) + -bar (“-able”).

noun:Lemma.tx: From the Latin lemma, from the Ancient Greek λῆμμᾰ (lêmmă).

noun:Libido.tx: Borrowed from Latin libīdō. The usual stress on the first syllable probably from a generalisation of the tendency that penultimate Latin -i- is short; perhaps also reinforced by association with Liebe (“love”), though this is speculative.

noun:Lettner.tx: From Middle High German lettener, lecter, from Latin lectorium.

verb:laichen.tx: From Middle High German leichen (“to jump, rise, mate, spawn”). Despite the late attestation (14th c.) plausibly inherited from Proto-West Germanic *laikan (“to jump, play”). Alternatively denominal from Middle High German leich. Equivalent to Laich + -en.

noun:Laich.tx: From Middle High German leich. Identical with Leich and thus ultimately from Proto-Germanic *laikaz (dance, game).

noun:Landstrich.tx: 17th century, from Land (“land”) + Strich (“stroke, stretch”). Compare Dutch streek (“region”).

noun:Lusche.tx: Unknown, possibly related to lasch (“slack, lax”), which is itself related to English lush.

noun:Leutnant.tx: From Middle French lieutenant (“lieutenant; deputy”), from tenir le lieu de (“to keep the position of”). Early on, the form was folk-etymologically reshaped, the first syllable being associated with Leute (“folk, men”), the last syllable sometimes with Amt (“post, office”). The normal spoken form in German has been Leut(e)nant since the 17th century, although the French spelling Lieutenant …

verb:leaken.tx: Borrowed from English leak, equivalent to Leak + -en. Doublet of lechen.

verb:losen.tx: From Middle High German lōzen, either derived from the noun lōz (whence German Los), or inherited from unattested Old High German *lōzōn, *hlōzōn, from Proto-West Germanic *hlutōn, from Proto-Germanic *hlutōną.

noun:Liegenschaft.tx: 19th century, from liegen (“to lie, be situated”) + -schaft, after older liegende Güter (literally “lying estates”).

verb:limitieren.tx: From Latin limitare or else French limiter.

verb:langen.tx: From Middle High German langen, from Old High German langēn, from Proto-West Germanic *langōn, from Proto-Germanic *langōną.

noun:Lustspiel.tx: Germanic translation of Komödie. Lust + Spiel.

noun:Limit.tx: Borrowed from English limit, ultimately from Latin līmes. Doublet of Limite.

verb:losgehen.tx: los- + gehen; cognate with Hunsrik losgehn

adj:letzte.tx: From Middle High German lest, a contraction of leȥȥest, from Old High German leȥȥist (also laȥȥōst), itself superlative of laȥ (cognate to English late). The modern German form with -tz- is of northern origin; two separate origins have probably met in it: Firstly, there is a general tendency in some Central German dialects of inserting -t- before comparative and superlative endings. (Compare for …

noun:Locked-in-Syndrom.tx: Naturalized loanword from English locked-in syndrome.

adj:läufig.tx: From Middle High German [Term?]. Cognate with Hunsrik leefich. Cognate with Old Saxon luvig, lubig (“willing”)

verb:lauten.tx: From Middle High German lūten (“to sound, ring”), from Old High German hlūtēn, from Proto-West Germanic *hlūdēn. Equivalent to Laut + -en. Cognate with Dutch luiden. The general sense was absorbed in Modern German by läuten, originally the factitive of lauten.

noun:Lacke.tx: From Middle High German lache, from Old High German lacha, lahha (“swamp, marsh”), from Proto-Germanic *lakō (“lake, pool”). See variant Lache for more.

noun:Lake.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German lāke, from Old Saxon laca, from Proto-West Germanic *laku, from Proto-Germanic *lakō (“lake, pool”). Originally the same word as Lache (“puddle”), which see for more.

noun:Leuchte.tx: From Middle High German liuhte, from Old High German liuhta, liohta.

noun:Lumineszenz.tx: Borrowed from English luminescence, from Latin lumen + English -escence.

noun:Lehrkraft.tx: From lehren (“to teach”) + Kraft (“worker, employee”, literally “force, [man]power”).

noun:Lapislazuli.tx: From Latin lapis lazuli, which see.

verb:lynchen.tx: Borrowed from English lynch, with a strongly Germanised spelling pronunciation (as is common in older loanwords).

noun:Lesart.tx: From lesen + Art, literally “way of reading”.

adj:landesweit.tx: From Land (“land, country, state”) + -es- + weit (“wide, far”).

verb:läuten.tx: From Middle High German liuten, from Old High German hlūten, from Proto-West Germanic *hlūdijan (“to make sound”), factitive of *hlūdēn (“to sound”), whence lauten. Equivalent to Laut + -en. Cognate with Dutch luiden. In Middle High German, the distinction between both verbs was increasingly lost, i.e. läuten came to be used intransitively. In Modern German, the two forms were then redistributed …

adj:lütt.tx: Borrowed from German Low German lütt, from Middle Low German lüttek, from Old Saxon luttik, from Proto-West Germanic *lūtil. Cognate with archaic German lützel, English little, Dutch luttel, Danish lille, Swedish/Norwegian liten. More at little.

noun:Linnen.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German linnen.

noun:Lakritz.tx: From Middle High German lakerize, from Old French licorece or directly from Medieval Latin, from Late Latin liquiritia, from Ancient Greek γλυκύρριζα (glukúrrhiza, “sweet root”).

verb:lispeln.tx: From Old High German lispen (“lisp”) + -eln, ultimately from onomatopoeic Proto-Germanic *wlispaz (“stammering, lisping”).

noun:Lebewohl.tx: From the farewell greeting lebe wohl! (“live well”).

adj:leibeigen.tx: From Middle High German līpeigen. Equivalent to Leib (“body”) + -eigen (“own, owned”).

noun:Lebenslüge.tx: From Leben (“life”) + -s- + Lüge (“lie”), calque of Danish livsløgn (coined by Ibsen in his 1884 play Vildanden).

adj:labberig.tx: Derived in the 18th century from labbern (“to be slack, to hang down (of sails)”), from German Low German [Term?]; compare Dutch labberen (“to hang slack”). Related to German laff (“slack; tasteless”).

adv:lauthals.tx: Borrowed from German Low German luudhals. By surface analysis, laut (“loud”) + Hals (“neck; throat”).

verb:lavieren.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German lavēren, from Middle Dutch laveren, loveren, which is derived from the cognate of German Luv (“windward side of the ship”). It is often supposed that the Dutch verb is borrowed from Middle French lofuyer, from lof (“windward side”), itself a Dutch borrowing in Middle French. The phonetics of the Dutch word speak in favour of this, but the earliest French …

noun:Lackmus.tx: From Dutch lakmoes, from Middle Dutch lecmoes, a compound of the cognates of German lecken (“to leak”) and Mus (“mush”). The former was later adapted to Dutch lak, German Lack (“varnish”). It seems obvious that there is a relation between Middle Dutch lecmoes and synonymous Old Norse litmosi (whence English litmus), but the nature of this relation is unsettled.

verb:lodern.tx: An originally Central and Low German verb, pertaining to Middle Low German lōde (“sapling”), and hence originally meaning “to grow upward”. The contemporary sense through association with unrelated Lohe (“flame”).

noun:Lure.tx: Of North Germanic origin, from Norwegian and Danish lur, from Old Norse lúðr.

noun:Litanei.tx: From Middle High German litanīe, from Late Latin litanīa, from Ancient Greek λιτανεία (litaneía).

noun:Leumund.tx: From Middle High German liumunt, from Old High German hliumunt, from Proto-Germanic *hleumundaz (“reputation”). Cognate with Sanskrit श्रोमत (śromata, “fame, renown, glory, celebrity”). The full vowel -u- in the unstressed syllable was preserved due to popular association with unrelated Mund (“mouth”).

verb:lugen.tx: From Middle High German luogen, from Old High German luogēn, from Proto-West Germanic *lōgēn (“to look, see”). Compare Alemannic German luege.

adj:lockig.tx: From an earlier lockicht, from Middle High German lockeht, analyzable as Locke (“curl”) + -ig.

verb:lallen.tx: From Middle High German lallen, lellen, from Old High German lallōn, lalōn, ultimately of imitative origin; compare Ancient Greek λάλος (lálos, “babbling”), and perhaps English Lollard.

noun:Lümmel.tx: From obsolete lumm (“loose, limp”), ultimately from the root of lahm (“lame”).

noun:Löffelliste.tx: Löffel (“spoon”) + Liste (“list”). The former word refers to the expression den Löffel abgeben (“to die”, literally “to hand in the spoon”). Calque of English bucket list, from kick the bucket.

noun:Leut.tx: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *liudīz (“people”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ- (“man, people”). See the more common term, Leute (“people”).

noun:Lesefähigkeit.tx: From lesen + Fähigkeit or Lesen + Fähigkeit.

noun:Leite.tx: From Middle High German līte, from Old High German hlīta, from Proto-West Germanic *hlīdu, from Proto-Germanic *hlīdō.

noun:Loh.tx: Middle High German lōch, Old High German lōh, from Proto-West Germanic *lauh.

noun:Lat.tx: Clipping of Latissimus dorsi, with structural borrowing from English lat.

noun:Loden.tx: From Middle High German lode, from Old High German lodo, ludo, derived from Proto-West Germanic *leudan, from Proto-Germanic *leudaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ-. Cognate with Old Norse loðinn (“hairy, furry”).

noun:Labskaus.tx: Probably from German Low German Lapskaus, from English lobscouse; origin uncertain.

adj:lasch.tx: 18th century, from Low German lasch, from Middle Low German lasch, las, from Old Saxon *lask, from Proto-West Germanic *laskw, from Proto-Germanic *laskwaz (“dull, lax, sluggish, lazy”). Likely influenced by French lâche, from Latin laxus.

adj:leidlich.tx: From Middle High German līdelich (“patient, enduring”, later also “endurable”). Analysable as leiden (“to suffer”) + -lich (“-ly, -able”); compare similar English sufferable. There was also another adjective, Middle High German leitlich (“painful, sorrowful”), from Old High German leidlīh, which, at least in spelling, was merged with the above in early modern German and which might have …

adv:leidlich.tx: From Middle High German līdelich (“patient, enduring”, later also “endurable”). Analysable as leiden (“to suffer”) + -lich (“-ly, -able”); compare similar English sufferable. There was also another adjective, Middle High German leitlich (“painful, sorrowful”), from Old High German leidlīh, which, at least in spelling, was merged with the above in early modern German and which might have …

adj:leinen.tx: From Middle High German līnīn. Equivalent to Lein (“flax, linen”) + -en.

adj:leiwand.tx: Regional variant of Leinwand (“linen, screen”, noun). According to one theory, coined in Vienna in the early 1900s when movie theaters were perceived as new and exotic. According to others, from a popular brand of beer.

adj:lichterloh.tx: From lichter Lohe (“with bright flame[s]”). Compare Dutch in lichterlaaie (“ablaze”).

adj:liederlich.tx: From Middle High German liederlich (“frivolous”, originally "slack, weak"), which Kluge compares to Ancient Greek ἐλεύθερος (eleútheros, “free”) (from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ- (“to grow”)). Pokorny prefers a derivation from Proto-Indo-European *(s)lew- (“slack; loose; limp”), see also Old Norse slokna (“to go out”). Compare Old Norse loddari (“juggler; tramp”), Old High German lotar (“vain; …

verb:lupfen.tx: From Middle High German lupfen, southern variant of lüpfen, whence modern lüpfen. See it for more.

noun:Lohe.tx: From Middle High German lohe, from Old High German *loho, a variant of loug, from Proto-West Germanic *laugi. Distantly related to Licht (“light”). Cognate with Swedish låga.

adj:leibhaftig.tx: From Middle High German līphaftic; equivalent to leibhaft + -ig. Related to Leib (“body”).

noun:Landmann.tx: From Old High German lantman, equivalent to Land + Mann.

noun:Leich.tx: Learned borrowing from Middle High German leich, from Old High German leih, from Proto-West Germanic *laik (“dance, game”). Cognate with Old English lac (“play, sport”), Middle Low German lēk and Swedish lek.

noun:Loggia.tx: Borrowed from Italian loggia. Doublet of Loge, Lobby, and Laube.

noun:Languste.tx: Borrowed from French langouste, from Latin locusta.

verb:lästern.tx: From Middle High German lestern, lastern, from Old High German lastarōn, derived from laster (“abuse, revilement”). Analysable as Laster + -n.

noun:Luder.tx: From Middle High German luoder, from Proto-Germanic *lōþr-. Perhaps related to Latin lateō (“to hide”) or from the same ultimate source as the verb laden (“to invite”), considering the sense of summoning, baiting.

verb:liebkosen.tx: From Middle High German liepkosen, equivalent to modern liebe (“dear”) + kosen (“to cuddle”).

noun:Labmagen.tx: Lab (“rennet”) + Magen (“maw”), for rennet is obtained from abomasa.

verb:losmachen.tx: los- + machen; cognate with Hunsrik losmache

verb:losbrechen.tx: los- + brechen; cognate with Hunsrik losbreche

verb:laben.tx: From Middle High German laben, from Old High German labōn, from Proto-West Germanic *labōn.

noun:Lyzeum.tx: From Latin Lycēum, from Ancient Greek Λύκειον (Lúkeion). The use for a girls’ school may have been partly due to an inhibition to using the word Gymnasium with girls because of the underlying Ancient Greek γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”).

noun:Labello.tx: From the brand name Labello, apparently a portmanteau word of Latin labium (“lip”) + bellus (“beautiful”), or similar forms in Romance languages such as Italian labbro + bello.

noun:Leumundszeugnis.tx: Leumund (“(someone's) reputation”) + Zeugnis (“testimony; certificate, report card”)

noun:Lotos.tx: Borrowed from Latin lotos, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós).

noun:Leibchen.tx: From Leib (“body”) + -chen. Compare Hunsrik Leibche, Austrian German Leiberl, Alemannic German Liibli. ===Pronunciation=== * IPA⁽ᵏᵉʸ⁾: /ˈlaɪ̯pçən/ * Audio (Germany (Berlin)): (file) * Homophone: Laibchen

noun:Lockenwickler.tx: From Locke (“curl”) + -n- + Wickler (“winder, coiler”), from wickeln (“to wrap, wind”).

noun:Landauer.tx: Origin of the carriage sense is uncertain, often assumed to be named after the city, Landau + -er.

noun:Löli.tx: Borrowed from Alemannic German Löli. Related to dialectal lollen, lallen (“to babble”).

verb:lechzen.tx: From Middle High German lechezen, an intensive form of Middle High German lechen

noun:Langmut.tx: 16th century back-formation from langmütig. Compare semantically equivalent Old High German langmuotī which was not continued.

adj:langmütig.tx: From Middle High German lancmüetec, from Old High German langmuotīg, formed from Old High German langmuot influenced by Ecclesiastical Latin longanimis. By surface analysis, Langmut + -ig.

verb:lungern.tx: From an earlier term meaning to "lurk, lie in wait for an opportunity", from Middle High German lunger (“greedy, active, brisk, quick”), from Old High German lungar (“quick, easy”), from Proto-West Germanic *lungur, from Proto-Germanic *lunguraz (“quick, vigorous, strong”). Alternatively from Middle Low German lungeren (“to eagerly lie in wait for, long for”) (compare Middle Low German lunger …

noun:Liebestöter.tx: Liebe (“love”) + -s- + Töter (“killer”), perhaps a calque of French tue-l'amour.

noun:Literaturkritiker.tx: From Literaturkritik + -er; equivalent to Literatur + Kritiker.

noun:Literaturwissenschaft.tx: From Literatur (“literature”) + Wissenschaft (“science”). Compare Dutch literatuurwetenschap.

noun:Lafette.tx: From Laffete, from L’Affuite (1665) and Affuiten (1617), from French l’affût (early 17tth century). Ultimately from Latin fūstis.

noun:Laufpass.tx: From laufen (“to run, go, walk”) + Pass (“pass, passport”). The colloquial sense is derived from the military one.

adj:lenz.tx: 19th century, from Dutch lens (“slack, empty”, also “dry”, of a ship). Further origin uncertain.

verb:legitimieren.tx: From Latin legitimare, ultimately from lēgitimus (“lawful, legal, legitimate”); equivalent to legitim + -ieren (“-ize, -ify”).

verb:letzen.tx: From Middle High German letzen, from Old High German lezzen, from Proto-Germanic *latjaną.

noun:Lesesaal.tx: Lesen + Saal. Compare Dutch leeszaal, Danish læsesal, Swedish läsesal.

noun:Lippfisch.tx: Lippe (“lip”) + Fisch (“fish”), on account of their prominent thick lips.

noun:Luch.tx: From Middle Low German lūch, from a West Slavic descendant of Proto-Slavic *lǫgъ (“depression”). Compare Upper Sorbian łuh and Czech luh.

noun:Luftikus.tx: Pseudo-Latinism from luftig + Latin -icus, -us, originally student slang.

noun:Ligatur.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin ligātūra, from Latin ligāre. Cognate with English ligature.

noun:Leuchtturmwärter.tx: From Leuchtturm (“lighthouse”) + Wärter (“attendant, keeper, guard, warder”).

noun:Leadgitarre.tx: Partial calque of English lead guitar, English lead + Gitarre.

noun:Leadgitarrist.tx: Partial calque of English lead guitarist, English lead + Gitarrist.

noun:Luftschutzbunker.tx: From Luftschutz + Bunker, from Luft (“air”) + Schutz (“protection”).

noun:Lichtbelästigung.tx: Tatpuruṣa compound of Licht + Belästigung, literally “harassment [by] light”. First attested in 1996.

noun:Lagerist.tx: 19th century, from Lager + -ist. Compare earlier formations like Kontorist (“clerk”), where the first component is a Latinate word.

adv:logischerweise.tx: From logisch + -erweise. Compare Yiddish לאָגישערווײַז (logishervayz), Dutch logischerwijs.

noun:Luxusproblem.tx: From Luxus (“luxury”) + Problem (“problem”). Compare Dutch luxeprobleem.

noun:Lenkwaffe.tx: From lenken (“to steer, drive; to navigate, guide”) + Waffe (“weapon”).

noun:Latsche.tx: Probably deverbal from latschen (“to traipse, walk about”), itself perhaps related with lasch (“slack”) or else onomatopoetic.

noun:Lichtschwert.tx: Calque of English lightsaber, from Licht (“light”) + Schwert (“sword”).

noun:Luxusgut.tx: From Luxus (“luxury”) + Gut (“commodity, property, possession, good”).

noun:Lattich.tx: From Middle High German latech, leteche, from Old High German latihha, lattuhha, from Latin lactuca (“lettuce”). Possibly through a Proto-West Germanic *ladukā ~ *lahtukā, though the wide variety of West Germanic forms makes such a reconstruction difficult.

noun:Laffe.tx: Inherited from Middle High German laffen or laffe. Perhaps ultimately related to laff (“insipid, stale”).

noun:Lordschaft.tx: Partial calque of English lordship, equivalent to Lord + -schaft.

noun:Legionär.tx: 19th century, from Legion + -är, after French légionnaire, from Latin legionarius.

noun:Lasur.tx: Middle High German lāsūr, lāsūre or lāzūr, lāzūre, from Medieval Latin lazurium, lazur, from Arabic لَازُوَرْد (lāzuward, “lapis lazuli, azure”), from Persian لاجورد (lâjvard).

noun:Lustgreis.tx: From Lust (“lust”) + Greis (“very old man, geriatric”).

noun:Lehmhaus.tx: Inherited from Middle High German, Old High German lêm-hûs. By surface analysis, Lehm + Haus. Compare Polish lamus.

noun:Laufzettel.tx: From laufen (“to run, go, walk”) + Zettel (“slip, paper”).

noun:Lausbub.tx: From Laus + Bub, from earlier Lauser.

noun:Ladyschaft.tx: Partial calque of English ladyship, equivalent to Lady + -schaft.

verb:längen.tx: From Middle High German lengen, from Old High German lengen, from Proto-West Germanic *langijan. By surface analysis, lang + -en.

noun:Leprechaun.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English leprechaun, from Irish leipreachán.

noun:Labung.tx: From Middle High German labunge, from Old High German labunga. By surface analysis, laben + -ung.

noun:Lokalität.tx: Latinized borrowing of French localité. By surface analysis, Lokal + -ität.

noun:Larifari.tx: From a sequence of solfège note names la, re, fa, re, with the modern meaning gained from describing as something akin to meaningless syllables used only for singing.

noun:Lebensbaum.tx: From Leben (“life”) + -s- + Baum (“tree”), literally “tree of life”, compare English tree of life and arborvitae.

noun:Leichenfledderer.tx: From Leiche (“corpse”) + -n- + fleddern (“to steal from the helpless”) + -er.

verb:laminieren.tx: From French laminer, ultimately from Latin lamina.

noun:Leichtgewicht.tx: Calque of English lightweight. By surface analysis, leicht + Gewicht.

noun:Larvenstadium.tx: From Larve (“larva”) + -n- + Stadium (“stage”). Cognate with Norwegian larvestadium.

noun:Lämmergeier.tx: From Lamm (“lamb”) + -er- + Geier (“vulture”), from the mistaken belief that it preyed on lambs.

noun:Liebesgras.tx: Calque of translingual Eragrostis, as Liebe (“love”) + -s- + Gras (“grass”).

noun:Liliputaner.tx: Calque of English lilliputian, equivalent to Liliput + -aner.

noun:Legitimation.tx: Borrowed from French légitimation, equivalent to legitimieren + -ation.

noun:Leiendecker.tx: By surface analysis, Lei (“slate”) + -en- + Decker (“coverer”). Compare Dutch leidekker.

noun:Lieblingsfächer.tx: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

adj:leckerschmecker.tx: From a 1970s chocolate bar of the same name, lecker + schmecken + -er.

noun:Lästermaul.tx: From lästern (“to bitch about”) + Maul (“muzzle, mouth”).

noun:Lidl.tx: The company is named after Anton Lidl, who founded it ca. 1856 in Heilbronn.
